title: Physiology, Nutrient Absorption -- Introduction
content: The gastrointestinal tract comprises a highly specialized organ system responsible for nutrient absorption, with additional roles in waste elimination, hormonal regulation, immune defense, and neurobehavioral modulation. Extending approximately 9 m (30 ft) from the mouth to the anus, the gut facilitates the breakdown and absorption of carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, and minerals, which are vital to energy production, growth, and cellular maintenance. Egestion of indigestible components and toxins maintains internal homeostasis.

title: Physiology, Nutrient Absorption -- Introduction
content: Endocrine signaling within the gastrointestinal tract regulates appetite, satiety, and metabolic processes. Immune cells within the gastrointestinal mucosa defend against pathogens while maintaining tolerance to commensal organisms. Neural and humoral signaling through the gut–brain axis exerts significant influence on behavior and cognitive function. [1] [2] [3] [4]

title: Physiology, Nutrient Absorption -- Introduction
content: Nutrient absorption is central to maintaining energy balance, growth, and cellular repair, and its disruption contributes to malnutrition, metabolic disorders, and systemic disease. Surgical procedures involving the stomach, small intestine, or pancreas frequently alter absorptive capacity, requiring careful perioperative planning and postoperative monitoring. Knowledge of the pathophysiology of nutrient absorption enables clinicians to anticipate complications, optimize nutritional support, and individualize treatment strategies.

title: Physiology, Nutrient Absorption -- Issues of Concern
content: Disorders affecting nutrient absorption encompass a wide spectrum of pathological mechanisms that impair the uptake of macronutrients and micronutrients, resulting in clinically significant short- and long-term consequences. These conditions are commonly classified into 3 major categories. Malabsorption syndromes arise from diseases of the small intestine, pancreas, liver, or biliary tract that disrupt the physiological processes necessary for digestion and absorption. [5] Micronutrient deficiencies frequently involve iron, vitamin B12, calcium, magnesium, and fat-soluble vitamins, with deficits producing clinically relevant hematologic, skeletal, and metabolic complications. [6] Dietary and host-related factors, including age, genetic variants, disease states, and gut microbiota composition, further modulate absorptive efficiency and influence clinical outcomes. [7]

title: Physiology, Nutrient Absorption -- Cellular Level
content: The gastrointestinal tract consists of multiple cell types, each dedicated to specific physiological roles. Disruption of these cellular functions contributes to enteric pathology.
contents: Physiology, Nutrient Absorption -- Cellular Level. The gastrointestinal tract consists of multiple cell types, each dedicated to specific physiological roles. Disruption of these cellular functions contributes to enteric pathology.

title: Physiology, Nutrient Absorption -- Cellular Level
content: Enterocytes constitute the majority of the intestinal epithelium and mediate the uptake of ions, water, nutrients, vitamins, and unconjugated bile acid salts. [8] Goblet cells, interspersed among enterocytes, are unicellular glands that secrete alkaline mucus to protect the gastrointestinal lining from mechanical stress and acidic secretions. [9] Enteroendocrine cells, distributed throughout the stomach, pancreas, and small intestine, secrete biogenic amines and polypeptides, including ghrelin, cholecystokinin, glucagon-like peptide 1, peptide YY, insulin-like peptide 5, and oxyntomodulin. These cells contribute to digestion, regulate nutrient absorption, and participate in immune surveillance by expressing toll-like receptors and specific molecular sensors for commensal bacterial metabolites. [10] [11]

title: Physiology, Nutrient Absorption -- Cellular Level
content: G-cells, located in the gastric antrum and duodenum, secrete gastrin, which stimulates enterochromaffin-like cells to release histamine and parietal cells to secrete hydrochloric acid. Gastrin additionally promotes gastric mucosal growth and motility. G-cells are innervated by the vagus nerve and activated by gastrin-releasing peptide and bombesin. [12] Oxyntic (parietal) cells, located in the gastric mucosa, secrete hydrochloric acid, which facilitates food breakdown, activates digestive enzymes, and maintains the low intragastric pH required for antimicrobial defense. These cells also produce intrinsic factor, essential for vitamin B12 absorption in the terminal ileum. [13]

title: Physiology, Nutrient Absorption -- Cellular Level
content: Zymogenic (chief) cells secrete pepsinogen, chymosin, and gastric lipase. Pepsinogen is converted to pepsin by hydrochloric acid. Both pepsin and chymosin catalyze protein breakdown into amino acids. [14] Paneth cells, situated in the crypts of Lieberkühn of the small and large intestine, secrete antimicrobial peptides and proteins that regulate intestinal microbiota and modulate inflammatory responses. [15] Microfold (M) cells within Peyer patches of the small intestine sample luminal antigens and deliver them to antigen-presenting cells, initiating mucosal immune responses. [16] Tuft cells, another specialized population of small intestinal epithelial cells, contribute to immune defense against parasitic and protozoal infections through chemosensory signaling and cytokine release. [17] [18]

title: Physiology, Nutrient Absorption -- Development
content: Gastrointestinal development begins in the 3rd week of embryogenesis, when the primordial digestive tract forms from the endodermal lining of the yolk sac in conjunction with its arterial blood supply. The primitive gut tube subsequently divides into the foregut, midgut, and hindgut.
contents: Physiology, Nutrient Absorption -- Development. Gastrointestinal development begins in the 3rd week of embryogenesis, when the primordial digestive tract forms from the endodermal lining of the yolk sac in conjunction with its arterial blood supply. The primitive gut tube subsequently divides into the foregut, midgut, and hindgut.

title: Physiology, Nutrient Absorption -- Development
content: The foregut, supplied by the celiac trunk, gives rise to the pharynx, esophagus, stomach, liver, gallbladder, bile ducts, pancreas, and proximal duodenum. The midgut, supplied by the superior mesenteric artery, develops into the distal duodenum, jejunum, ileum, cecum, ascending colon, and proximal 2/3 of the transverse colon. The hindgut, supplied by the inferior mesenteric artery, forms the distal 1/3 of the transverse colon, descending colon, sigmoid colon, rectum, and proximal anal canal. Although organogenesis is complete by the 8th week, functional intestinal absorption begins around the 24th week of gestation. [19]

title: Physiology, Nutrient Absorption -- Development
content: Congenital anomalies such as atresia and stenosis result from disruptions in embryologic development. The impact on digestion and absorption depends on the specific location and severity of the defect. [20]

title: Physiology, Nutrient Absorption -- Organ Systems Involved
content: The gastrointestinal system maintains extensive interactions with all other organ systems. Communication with the nervous system occurs through hormonal signaling and the enteric nervous system, which regulates motility, secretion, and reflex activity. [21] Gastrointestinal circulation supports multiple essential functions, including delivery of oxygen, nutrients, and regulatory substances to gastrointestinal tissues, absorption and transport of nutrients into the systemic circulation, clearance of cellular metabolites, maintenance of hemodynamic stability, and modulation of peripheral vascular tone. [22]

title: Physiology, Nutrient Absorption -- Organ Systems Involved
content: The gastrointestinal and renal systems work together to maintain calcium homeostasis. The kidneys convert 25-hydroxyvitamin D into its active form, 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D, which stimulates colonic absorption of calcium and phosphate. Renal disease or nutritional deficiencies disrupt this process, leading to calcium imbalance and bone disorders. [23] Gastrointestinal absorption of vitamins and minerals is equally critical for musculoskeletal integrity. Impaired absorption of vitamin D, calcium, magnesium, or phosphate results in bone loss, inflammation, and musculoskeletal pain. [24]

title: Physiology, Nutrient Absorption -- Organ Systems Involved
content: Several physiologic mechanisms demonstrate the interplay between the pulmonary and gastrointestinal systems. Adequate oxygenation of gastrointestinal tissues is required for optimal cellular metabolism. Intestinal absorption of iron is essential for hemoglobin synthesis and systemic oxygen delivery. Hepatic dysfunction, as in cirrhosis, may result in portal hypertension and ascites, which can progress to hepatic hydrothorax and pleural effusion. [25] [26]

title: Physiology, Nutrient Absorption -- Organ Systems Involved
content: The gastrointestinal system also fulfills essential endocrine functions. Pancreatic β-cells secrete insulin, while α-cells secrete glucagon. Both hormones regulate blood glucose homeostasis and energy expenditure. Intestinal absorption of cholesterol provides the substrate for steroid hormone biosynthesis, linking gastrointestinal function to endocrine activity. [27] This connection extends to reproduction, as sex hormones are steroid-based molecules derived from cholesterol and its intermediates. [28]

title: Physiology, Nutrient Absorption -- Function -- Mouth
content: The mouth consists of the lips, teeth, tongue, salivary glands, hard and soft palates, uvula, and oropharynx. The lips are mobile, fleshy structures that surround the oral opening and are essential for speech, facial expression, and creating an effective seal during eating and drinking. The teeth mechanically break down food into smaller particles to facilitate digestion, while also contributing to oral cavity protection and articulation of speech.

title: Physiology, Nutrient Absorption -- Function -- Mouth
content: The tongue, a muscular organ on the floor of the oral cavity, is responsible for taste perception, bolus manipulation, initiation of swallowing, and triggering the gag reflex. [29] Salivary glands within and around the oral cavity secrete saliva, which contains amylase to initiate carbohydrate digestion and lysozyme to provide antimicrobial defense. [30] The palate forms the roof of the mouth, separating the oral and nasal cavities and aiding mastication and deglutition. The uvula, a small projection of the soft palate, prevents nasopharyngeal regurgitation during swallowing. [31]

title: Physiology, Nutrient Absorption -- Function -- Esophagus
content: The esophagus is anatomically divided into 3 segments. The upper 1/3 consists primarily of striated muscle under voluntary somatic control. The middle 1/3 contains a mixture of striated and smooth muscle. The lower 1/3 is composed predominantly of smooth muscle regulated by autonomic innervation.

title: Physiology, Nutrient Absorption -- Function -- Esophagus
content: The mucosal lining consists of nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium, which protects against mechanical stress during swallowing. Propulsion of food from the mouth to the stomach occurs through coordinated muscular contractions known as peristalsis.

title: Physiology, Nutrient Absorption -- Function -- Esophagus
content: Two physiologic sphincters regulate bolus transit and prevent reflux. The cervical esophagus, cricopharyngeus, and inferior pharyngeal constrictor muscles form the upper esophageal sphincter. [32] The lower esophageal sphincter consists of the diaphragmatic crura, phrenoesophageal ligament, and intrinsic esophageal muscle fibers. [33]

title: Physiology, Nutrient Absorption -- Function -- Stomach
content: The stomach is divided into 5 anatomical regions: cardia, fundus, body, antrum, and pylorus. The cardia forms the junction with the esophagus and contains a sphincteric mechanism that prevents reflux of gastric contents. The fundus, located inferior to the cardia, serves as a reservoir for ingested material. The body constitutes the largest portion of the stomach and functions as the primary site where food is mixed with gastric secretions. The antrum, the distal portion of the stomach, temporarily holds the chyme before its regulated release into the small intestine. The pylorus, which connects the stomach to the duodenum, contains a thick muscular sphincter that controls gastric emptying. The stomach also serves as the first site of absorption for lipid-soluble substances, including alcohol and aspirin. [34]

title: Physiology, Nutrient Absorption -- Function -- Small Intestine
content: The small intestine is divided into 3 segments: the duodenum, jejunum, and ileum. The duodenum, approximately 30 cm (1 ft) long, forms the proximal segment and receives the gastric chyme. Secretions from the liver, pancreas, and gallbladder mix with the chyme in this segment to facilitate enzymatic digestion. The duodenum is the primary site for absorption of iron, calcium, phosphorus, magnesium, copper, selenium, thiamin, riboflavin, niacin, biotin, folate, and the fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E, and K. Numerous intestinal villi increase the epithelial surface area, optimizing nutrient uptake. [35]

title: Physiology, Nutrient Absorption -- Function -- Small Intestine
content: The jejunum, approximately 244 cm (8 ft) long, forms the middle segment of the small intestine and is the principal site for absorption of most nutrients. Jejunal lacteals absorb lipids that have been hydrolyzed into glycerol and free fatty acids, while amino acids enter the bloodstream via the mesenteric capillaries. [36] Additional nutrients absorbed in the jejunum include thiamine, riboflavin, niacin, pantothenate, biotin, folate, pyridoxine, ascorbic acid, calcium, phosphorus, magnesium, iron, zinc, chromium, manganese, molybdenum, monosaccharides, small peptides, and fat-soluble vitamins.

title: Physiology, Nutrient Absorption -- Function -- Small Intestine
content: The ileum, approximately 150 cm (5 ft) long, constitutes the distal portion of the small intestine and terminates at the ileocecal junction. This segment is primarily responsible for the absorption of bile salts, bile acids, cobalamin, folate, ascorbic acid, vitamin D, vitamin K, and magnesium. [37]

title: Physiology, Nutrient Absorption -- Function -- Large Intestine
content: The large intestine extends from the ileocecal valve superiorly to the anus inferiorly and comprises the ascending colon, transverse colon, descending colon, rectum, and anus. The primary functions of this segment include water absorption, stool formation, and fecal elimination. [38]

title: Physiology, Nutrient Absorption -- Mechanism
content: Digestion is the physiologic process by which food is converted into absorbable products that provide nourishment. Mechanical digestion physically breaks food into smaller fragments through mastication, deglutition, churning, and segmentation. Chemical digestion further deconstructs these fragments into absorbable molecules through pH-dependent reactions and enzymatic activity. [39]

title: Physiology, Nutrient Absorption -- Mechanism
content: Nutrient absorption occurs through cellular transport via 2 principal pathways. In the paracellular pathway, molecules move passively from the intestinal lumen across tight junctions between epithelial cells and into the interstitium. This process is unmediated and driven by electrochemical concentration gradients. In the transcellular pathway, molecules cross the apical membrane to enter the enterocyte, traverse the cytoplasm, and exit across the basolateral membrane into the interstitial space. Unlike the paracellular route, transcellular transport requires energy in the form of adenosine triphosphate (ATP) and is facilitated by apical and basolateral membrane transporters. [40] [41] Although paracellular transport plays a relatively minor role in glucose absorption, the transcellular pathway accounts for the majority of nutrient uptake.

title: Physiology, Nutrient Absorption -- Mechanism
content: Once absorbed into the interstitium, nutrients enter the venous portal system. Blood from the villous capillaries transports these molecules from the gastrointestinal tract to the liver, where hepatocytes further metabolize, store, and distribute nutrients systemically via the inferior vena cava (see Image . Small Intestinal Villi Schematic Representation). Most nutrients reach the bloodstream through paracellular and transcellular transport pathways, whereas lipids and fat-soluble vitamins are absorbed into specialized lymphatic vessels, the lacteals, for systemic distribution.

title: Physiology, Nutrient Absorption -- Mechanism
content: Lipids absorbed by the lacteals enter the intestinal lymphatic network and converge in the cisterna chyli, located in the retrocrural space, which serves as the abdominal origin of the thoracic duct.  In approximately 95% of cases, the thoracic duct subsequently drains into the internal jugular vein, subclavian vein, or the junction between these 2 blood vessels. The remaining lymph may enter the external jugular, vertebral, brachiocephalic, suprascapular, or transverse cervical veins (see Image . Thoracic Lymphatic System). [42]

title: Physiology, Nutrient Absorption -- Pathophysiology -- Carbohydrate Absorption
content: Carbohydrate digestion starts in the oral cavity through mechanical breakdown. Chemical digestion begins when mechanically processed food encounters enzymes from the salivary glands, pancreas, and intestinal brush border. Enzymatic hydrolysis of glycosidic bonds converts complex carbohydrates into monosaccharides, primarily glucose, fructose, and galactose, which are subsequently absorbed into the bloodstream via transcellular transport.

title: Physiology, Nutrient Absorption -- Pathophysiology -- Carbohydrate Absorption
content: Transcellular uptake begins at the apical membrane of enterocytes with the sodium-glucose cotransporter 1 (SGLT1), which couples the transport of glucose or galactose to 2 sodium ions. This process is driven by a sodium gradient established by basolateral sodium-potassium ATPase pumps, representing secondary active transport. Fructose absorption occurs through the apical glucose transporter 5 (GLUT5), which facilitates passive entry via facilitated diffusion due to its high affinity for fructose. Monosaccharides exit the enterocyte through the basolateral membrane via glucose transporter 2 (GLUT2), allowing glucose, galactose, and fructose to enter the interstitial space by facilitated diffusion. [43]

title: Physiology, Nutrient Absorption -- Pathophysiology -- Carbohydrate Absorption
content: Carbohydrates that resist enzymatic digestion, such as cellulose, remain in the colon and undergo fermentation by colonic microbiota. This process contributes to short-chain fatty acid production and gut microbial metabolism.

title: Physiology, Nutrient Absorption -- Pathophysiology -- Protein Absorption
content: Chemical protein digestion begins in the stomach and continues through the jejunum. [44] Peptidases secreted by the stomach, pancreas, and intestinal brush border hydrolyze polypeptides into dipeptides, tripeptides, and free amino acids.

title: Physiology, Nutrient Absorption -- Pathophysiology -- Protein Absorption
content: Protein absorption primarily occurs in the jejunum and proximal ileum. Dipeptides and tripeptides enter the enterocyte cytoplasm via the proton-dependent peptide transporter 1 (PepT1), a high-capacity, low-affinity transporter that cotransports oligopeptides with hydrogen ions. Within the enterocyte, lysosomal enzymes further hydrolyze oligopeptides into single amino acids, which then cross the basolateral membrane to enter the interstitial space. [45] Free amino acids in the lumen are absorbed through sodium-linked facilitated diffusion via multiple apical membrane transporters, which often exhibit overlapping substrate specificities. For example, system B cotransports neutral amino acids with sodium ions.

content: After entry into the cytoplasm, single amino acids cross the basolateral membrane to enter the extracellular space. These molecules are then transported via the venous portal system to the liver, as previously described. [46] [47]

title: Physiology, Nutrient Absorption -- Pathophysiology -- Fat Absorption
content: Lipid digestion begins in the oral cavity with salivary lipase, which hydrolyzes triglycerides into monoglycerides, glycerol, and free fatty acids. Gastric and pancreatic lipases continue lipid breakdown throughout the stomach and small intestine. Bile secreted by the gallbladder facilitates lipase activity by emulsifying fats in the terminal duodenum and jejunum. Digested lipids aggregate in the lumen to form micelles. Absorption occurs when individual lipid molecules diffuse across the enterocyte apical membrane. [48]

title: Physiology, Nutrient Absorption -- Pathophysiology -- Fat Absorption
content: Within enterocytes, fatty acids cross the basolateral membrane and enter the venous portal system. Monoglycerides are reesterified in the endoplasmic reticulum to form triglycerides, which are packaged into chylomicrons. These chylomicrons incorporate lipoproteins and long-chain fatty acids, exit the enterocyte at the basolateral surface, and enter the lacteals. Lymphatic propulsion, aided by thoracic muscle contractions, transports chylomicron-rich lymph superiorly until it drains into the systemic circulation via the right subclavian vein. [49] Lipids undergo conversion for energy storage, insulation, or steroid hormone synthesis once delivered to tissues. [50]

title: Physiology, Nutrient Absorption -- Pathophysiology -- Fat Absorption
content: Duodenal hormones, including secretin and cholecystokinin, regulate lipid digestion by reducing intestinal motility. These hormones simultaneously stimulate pancreatic and gallbladder secretions, enhancing enzymatic activity and fat emulsification. Vitamins and Minerals

title: Physiology, Nutrient Absorption -- Pathophysiology -- Fat Absorption
content: Vitamins A, D, E, and K are fat-soluble and readily dissolve in lipids and other nonpolar solvents. [51] In the small intestine, these vitamins integrate into micelles and cross the enterocyte apical membrane via simple diffusion. Within the enterocyte, the absorbed vitamins are incorporated into chylomicrons and subsequently enter the systemic circulation. Fat-soluble vitamins are predominantly stored in adipose tissue, where they can persist for extended periods. Chronic excessive intake of these micronutrients may result in toxicity.

title: Physiology, Nutrient Absorption -- Pathophysiology -- Fat Absorption
content: Water-soluble vitamins include thiamine (B1), riboflavin (B2), niacin (B3), pantothenic acid (B5), pyridoxine (B6), biotin (B7), folic acid (B9), cobalamin (B12), and ascorbic acid (C). [52] These vitamins are absorbed through specific carrier-mediated pathways rather than passive diffusion. Following absorption, these nutrients are distributed to tissues to support metabolic processes. Excess water-soluble vitamins reaching supratherapeutic levels are excreted by the kidneys, minimizing the risk of accumulation and toxicity. However, the limited storage of these essential nutrients necessitates regular dietary replenishment. [53]

title: Physiology, Nutrient Absorption -- Clinical Significance
content: Malabsorption arises when the gastrointestinal tract fails to absorb nutrients effectively, frequently resulting from underlying gastrointestinal disease. The most prevalent causes in the U.S. are pancreatic insufficiency, celiac disease, and Crohn disease. [54]

title: Physiology, Nutrient Absorption -- Clinical Significance
content: Malabsorptive conditions disrupt luminal, mucosal, or postabsorptive processes. Luminal impairment limits mechanical digestion and enzymatic hydrolysis necessary to convert food into absorbable molecules. [55] Mucosal defects decrease nutrient transport across enterocyte membranes. Postabsorptive dysfunction compromises nutrient distribution through the lymphatic and portal systems. Clinical manifestations depend on the specific nutrient deficiency and the extent of intestinal compromise.

title: Physiology, Nutrient Absorption -- Clinical Significance
content: Surgical shortening of the intestines reduces transit time for nutrient absorption and can precipitate malabsorptive symptoms. [56] Residual intestinal surface area directly determines the efficiency of nutrient uptake.

title: Physiology, Nutrient Absorption -- Clinical Significance -- Carbohydrate Malabsorption
content: The large intestine receives unabsorbed carbohydrates, which are metabolized by anaerobic colonic bacteria through fermentation processes. Fermentation produces gas, which, in excess, can provoke abdominal cramping and bloating.
contents: Physiology, Nutrient Absorption -- Clinical Significance -- Carbohydrate Malabsorption. title: Physiology, Nutrient Absorption -- Clinical Significance -- Carbohydrate Malabsorption
content: Lactase deficiency impairs the digestion of lactose-containing foods, such as dairy products. [57] This condition affects approximately 65% of the global population and results from insufficient or structurally defective lactase within the gut. Unabsorbed lactose reaching the colon generates osmotic and fermentative effects, producing abdominal pain and diarrhea following lactose ingestion.

title: Physiology, Nutrient Absorption -- Clinical Significance -- Carbohydrate Malabsorption
content: Celiac disease constitutes another cause of carbohydrate malabsorption. Gluten exposure in susceptible individuals triggers an immune-mediated reaction that damages the intestinal mucosa. Villous atrophy and brush border blunting reduce the small intestine’s absorptive capacity.

title: Physiology, Nutrient Absorption -- Clinical Significance -- Carbohydrate Malabsorption
content: In pediatric patients, carbohydrate malabsorption manifests as chronic caloric deficiency, weight loss, and impaired growth. Concomitant malabsorption of other nutrients frequently occurs, leading to additional nutritional deficiencies. [58]

title: Physiology, Nutrient Absorption -- Clinical Significance -- Protein Malabsorption
content: Impaired protein absorption rarely occurs in isolation and typically constitutes a component of global malabsorptive conditions. Protein deficiency disrupts multiple physiological processes, including the absorption and utilization of other nutrients.

title: Physiology, Nutrient Absorption -- Clinical Significance -- Protein Malabsorption
content: Insufficient protein impairs lipoprotein aggregation, a process essential for lipid and cholesterol metabolism. Hypoalbuminemia diminishes plasma transport capacity for fat-soluble vitamins, hormones, and pharmacologic agents, while simultaneously reducing plasma oncotic pressure, which promotes 3rd-spacing and edema formation. [59] [60]

title: Physiology, Nutrient Absorption -- Clinical Significance -- Protein Malabsorption
content: Severe protein malabsorption may result in Kwashiorkor syndrome, characterized by edema, skin and hair abnormalities, hepatomegaly, and ascites due to impaired hepatic apoprotein synthesis. Immunoglobulin production is compromised, increasing susceptibility to infections. [61] Chronic protein deficiency from any etiology can lead to profound complications and mortality. [62]

title: Physiology, Nutrient Absorption -- Clinical Significance -- Fat Malabsorption
content: Fat malabsorption primarily results from impaired interaction between lipolytic enzymes, bile, and dietary lipids in partially digested chyme. Common etiologies include pancreatic exocrine insufficiency, biliary obstruction, postsurgical anatomical alterations (eg, following a Whipple procedure), intestinal mucosal injury, and gastrointestinal motility disorders.

title: Physiology, Nutrient Absorption -- Clinical Significance -- Fat Malabsorption
content: Pancreatic exocrine insufficiency denotes the inability of the pancreas to secrete digestive enzymes, electrolytes, and water. Intestinal mucosal damage may arise from inflammatory disorders, radiation exposure, or infectious processes.

title: Physiology, Nutrient Absorption -- Clinical Significance -- Fat Malabsorption
content: Clinical manifestations of fat malabsorption include loose, bulky, clay-colored stools with a tendency to float, unintentional weight loss, fatigue, and generalized weakness. Deficiencies of fat-soluble vitamins can develop, presenting with osteopenia or osteoporosis, night blindness, coagulopathy, and, in rare cases, hemolytic anemia. [63]

title: Physiology, Nutrient Absorption -- Clinical Significance -- Malnutrition in Hospitalized Patients and the Critically Ill
content: Nutritional support is critical when caring for hospitalized patients. Critical conditions, such as sepsis, shock, and malignancy, frequently induce intestinal hypomotility, anorexia, and hypermetabolic states. Preoperative fasting is commonly recommended for surgical patients prior to sedation to reduce aspiration risk. [64] Inadequate nutritional support increases susceptibility to malnutrition-related complications, including hyponatremia, starvation ketoacidosis, and refeeding syndrome.

title: Physiology, Nutrient Absorption -- Clinical Significance -- Malnutrition in Hospitalized Patients and the Critically Ill
content: Current evidence does not demonstrate a mortality benefit associated with modified hospital diets, and overly restrictive regimens may be counterproductive. Early enteral feeding has not consistently shown improved clinical outcomes, whereas prolonged avoidance of enteric nutrition increases dependence on parenteral or alternative feeding modalities. [65]
